title: Generic reducedness of flat coefficient models under dominating domain base change
statement: Let $R$ and $D$ be finitely generated commutative $\mathbf Q$-algebras which are integral domains (nonzero rings with no zero divisors), and let $R\hookrightarrow D$ be an injective homomorphism of $\mathbf Q$-algebras. Let $B$ be a finite type $R$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra] flat as an $R$-module [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map]. Let $k$ be a field of characteristic zero equipped with an injective $\mathbf Q$-algebra map $R\hookrightarrow k$. Equip tensor products [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] with their usual algebra multiplication $(u\otimes b)(v\otimes c)=uv\otimes bc$. If $k\otimes_R B$ is generically reduced, then $D\otimes_R B$ is generically reduced. Here a ring $T$ is generically reduced if for every minimal prime $\mathfrak p$ of $T$ the localization $T_{\mathfrak p}$ has no nonzero nilpotent element [def-pc-reduced-scheme]; the zero ring is allowed, with this condition vacuous.

source.place: Tags 00HS (lemma-flat-going-down) and 030V (lemma-geometrically-reduced-finite-purely-inseparable-extension); combined generic-local consequence, including descent from a containing field, rather than a verbatim statement of either tag.

proof.text: Put $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ and $L=\operatorname{Frac}(D)$, the rings of fractions at nonzero elements. The given injections extend uniquely to $K\hookrightarrow k$ and $K\hookrightarrow L$ by $r/s\mapsto i(r)/i(s)$. Put $A=K\otimes_R B$, $T=D\otimes_R B$, and $C=L\otimes_R B$. The tensor-algebra universal property gives $k\otimes_K A\simeq k\otimes_R B$ and $L\otimes_K A\simeq C$: in either case $x\otimes(y\otimes b)\mapsto xy\otimes b$, with inverse $z\otimes b\mapsto z\otimes(1\otimes b)$. These formulas preserve multiplication and compose to the identity on pure tensors, hence on their sums.

source.place: Basic algebra conventions and fraction/tensor constructions; explicit reassociation maps.

proof.text: The fraction field $K$ has characteristic zero. Apply [lem-per-field-extension-generic-reducedness] to $K\hookrightarrow k$ and the $K$-algebra $A$. The first identification and the hypothesis give generic reducedness of $A$. Apply the same lemma to $K\hookrightarrow L$; the second identification gives generic reducedness of $C$. Both applications allow an arbitrary field extension and the zero algebra.

The $D$-module $T=D\otimes_RB$, with $D$ acting through the first factor, is flat by [lem-weil-pbc-flat-module-base-change] applied to $R\to D$ and the flat $R$-module $B$. Let $\mathfrak q$ be any minimal prime of $T$. Going down [lem-sc-flat-going-down] for the flat map $D\to T$, $d\mapsto d\otimes1$, applied to the primes $(0)\subseteq\mathfrak q\cap D$ of $D$ ($(0)$ is prime since $D$ is a domain; $\mathfrak q\cap D$ denotes the inverse image of $\mathfrak q$), gives a prime $\mathfrak q_1\subseteq\mathfrak q$ of $T$ contracting to $(0)$. Minimality forces $\mathfrak q_1=\mathfrak q$. Thus $\mathfrak q\cap D=(0)$.

source.place: Tag 00HI (lemma-flat-base-change) for flatness of the base change; Tag 00HS (lemma-flat-going-down).

proof.text: Let $S=D\setminus\{0\}$. Localization of the first tensor factor identifies $C$ with $S^{-1}T$; the module isomorphism preserves multiplication on fractions. Since $\mathfrak q\cap S=\varnothing$, the localization spectrum embedding gives a prime $\mathfrak q_S$ of $C$ contracting to $\mathfrak q$. It is minimal: a smaller prime contracts to a prime contained in $\mathfrak q$, hence to $\mathfrak q$, and injectivity of the spectrum embedding forces equality. There is an isomorphism $C_{\mathfrak q_S}\simeq T_{\mathfrak q}$ sending $(t/s)/(u/v)$ to $tv/(su)$; here $s,v\in S$ and $u\notin\mathfrak q$. Its inverse sends $t/u$ to $(t/1)/(u/1)$, and equality is the usual fraction equality. Since $C$ is generically reduced, $T_{\mathfrak q}$ is reduced. This holds for every minimal prime of $T$; if $T=0$, there are none.

source.place: Tag 00E3 (lemma-spec-localization), followed by the explicit two-stage localization fractions.
